source_text: Verumtamen nec virtutum est aerumnosa possessio, quae extra regnum quoddam bonae conscientiae promissa aeternae beatitudinis sublimitate fruitur; adsunt tamen adiutoria gratiae Dei, quae in parte virtutis numquam destituunt voluntatem, cuius licet innumerae species, tali tamen, semper moderatione adhibentur, ut numquam liberum arbitrium loco pellant, sed praebeant amminicula, quamdiu eis voluerit inniti, cum tamen non opprimant reluctantem animum. Inde quippe est, quod ut alii ad virtutes a vitiis ascendunt, ita etiam alii ad vitia a virtutibus relabuntur.
pass_a_gloss: Nevertheless neither is the possession of virtues toilsome, which outside a certain kingdom of good conscience enjoys the promised sublimity of eternal beatitude; yet the helps of the grace of God are present, which on the part of virtue never desert the will, whose species although innumerable are nevertheless always applied with such moderation that they never drive free choice from its place, but provide supports as long as it has wanted to lean on them, when nevertheless they do not oppress a reluctant mind. From there indeed it is that as some ascend to virtues from vices, so also others slide back to vices from virtues.

lemmas.lexica: LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'

pass_b_english: Yet possessing virtues is not a wretched business. Besides a kind of kingdom in a good conscience, it enjoys the promised height of eternal blessedness. The aids of God’s grace are also present, never abandoning the will on virtue’s side. Although grace has countless forms, they are always applied with such restraint that they never displace free will. They offer support for as long as the will chooses to lean on them, without overpowering a resistant mind. That is why, just as some people rise from vices to virtues, others also fall back from virtues to vices.

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
